newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania - a melting pot in heart of Balkans.
newsitem.headline: Albania - a melting pot in heart of Balkans.

text.p: Albania, scene of explosive violence since the start of year, is a political, religious and cultural melting pot in the heart of the troubled Balkans.

From the mountains of the north to fertile farming land in the south, Albania is home to a mixed 3.4 million population of Moslems, Orthodox Christians and Roman Catholics, native Albanians and ethnic Greeks.
"Religion in Albania is love of Albania," is a saying here.
The Shkumbin River, that cuts westwards across central Albania then flows into the Adriatic, marks a perceived division line across the country, locals say.
Dialects to the north and south of the Shkumbin are distinctive and villages within a few miles of one another have their own traditions, dress and customs.

Armed insurrection, following protests triggered by the collapse of a string of fraudulent investment schemes in January, has centred in the more affluent south, home to a sizeable ethnic Greek minority.

Since Monday, troops have been pressing down through the "bread basket of Albania", the verdant farming region that sweeps away from the capital, in a bid to quash unrest that has gripped some southern towns.

Resistance centred on the Adriatic port of Vlore has shown no sign of ebbing. People there are proud of a fighting tradition reinforced in 1912 when Albania declared its independence in the town, ending 450 years of Ottoman rule.
Stalinist leader Enver Hoxha, dictator to Europe's most isolated state for 40 years until his death in 1985, relied on Vlore to supply a steady flow of military officers for his communist army.
Today Vlore and the neighbouring towns of Berat, Tepelene, Fier and Gjirokaster are considered a fiefdom of the opposition Socialists, reformed heirs to the communists.
Southern partisans fought to liberate Albania from Nazi occupation in World War Two.
At least 80,000 ethnic Greeks live around Sarande, a short ferry ride from the Greek holiday island of Corfu, and in the town of Gjirokaster.

Support for Tirana's rightist Democratic Party is strongest in the homeland of President Sali Berisha -- the mountainous region to the north of the capital near the border with Yugoslavia, and in parts of central Albania.
Despite intense poverty and little infrastructure, people in the northern mountains have not reacted violently to the pyramid scheme crisis.

The main town of Shkoder, at the edge of Lake Shkoder that Albania shares with Montenegro, has remained calm despite rising unemployment and a loss of smuggling income that coincided with the lifting of international sanctions against Yugoslavia.
